lesson.title: Undoing the Secant: The Arcsec Integral Pattern
lesson.summary: The integral of 1/(x√(x²-1)) is arcsec(x) + C for x greater than 1, the trickiest of the three inverse trig integrals because of how its domain restricts to values with absolute value greater than 1.
lesson.body:
The arcsec integral rounds out the family, and it behaves a little differently from the other two because of where arcsec(x) is even defined. Since sec(y) = x requires |x| to be at least 1, you cannot get a secant value strictly between -1 and 1, arcsec(x) only makes sense for |x| at least 1, and its derivative is d/dx[arcsec(x)] = 1/(|x|√(x²-1)) for |x| > 1. Reading that in reverse, and restricting attention to x > 1 where |x| = x, gives the integral of 1/(x√(x²-1)) dx equals arcsec(x) + C. Textbooks commonly write this as arcsec|x| + C so the same formula also covers the x < -1 branch, but in most course work you apply it on x > 1, where the absolute value does not change anything.

The general version, with a positive constant a in place of 1, is: the integral of 1/(x√(x²-a²)) dx equals (1/a) arcsec(x/a) + C, for x > a. As with the arctan formula, do not forget the leading 1/a factor when a is not 1.

Evaluate the integral of 1/(x√(x²-1)) dx from x = √2 to x = 2. The antiderivative is arcsec(x), so the definite integral equals arcsec(2) minus arcsec(√2). To find arcsec(2), ask what angle has secant 2, which is the same as asking what angle has cosine 1/2: that angle is π/3 (60 degrees), since sec(π/3) = 1/cos(π/3) = 1/(1/2) = 2. To find arcsec(√2), ask what angle has cosine 1/√2: that angle is π/4 (45 degrees), since sec(π/4) = 1/cos(π/4) = 1/(√2/2) = 2/√2 = √2. So the integral equals π/3 minus π/4. Writing both over a common denominator of 12 gives 4π/12 minus 3π/12, which is π/12, about 0.2618.

The reason this integral is the one students find least intuitive is the domain restriction: you can only use it where x is greater than 1, or greater than a in the general form, because the expression under the square root, x² minus 1, would be negative otherwise and the integrand would not be a real number. Before applying this formula, always confirm your interval of integration stays entirely inside that domain, the way the interval from √2 to 2 does here, since both endpoints exceed 1.

This pattern completes the set introduced by the inverse trig integrals overview: three algebraic shapes, each one the mirror image of a derivative you already know, arcsin's, arctan's, and now arcsec's. The underlying logic never changes: an indefinite integral is a family of antiderivatives, and each of these three formulas is simply that idea applied to one particular inverse trig derivative.
